title: Two birds on one tree
hookLine: one bird eats the fruit, one bird only watches; when the lake goes still, who is looking?
carry: you are the seer, not your weather
tomorrow: five kinds of thought, and one of them is sleep?

cards: Two birds, close friends, sit on the same tree. One hops from branch to branch eating the fruit, sweet ones, bitter ones, and every bite changes its mood. A sweet one, and it's thrilled.
A bitter one, and it's miserable. The other bird eats nothing. It just watches, calm.

Then, now and then, the eating bird, sick of the bitter fruit, looks up and sees its friend, and its sorrow falls away. That's a picture from the Upanishads, and Hindus have handed it down for thousands of years.

teach.b: Patanjali's next two threads say it in yoga's language. Thread three: tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam. Then, when the turnings are still, the seer rests in its own nature.
Drashta, the seer, the one who sees. Thread four says what happens otherwise: the seer takes the shape of the turnings. The anger arrives, and you become angry.

teach.h: A CRYSTAL NEXT TO A RED FLOWER.
teach.b: Teachers use a crystal: set a clear crystal by a red flower and it looks red. It never was.
This is one of Hinduism's big teachings: you are not your thoughts.
Patanjali, leaning on the related Samkhya school, calls the seer purusha, pure awareness, and puts the body and even the mind on the other side, among the things seen.
The Upanishads call what's underneath atman, the self, and many teachers call it the sakshi, the witness. The schools describe it differently.
In the Upanishad, the watching bird is usually read as the Lord, or the highest self; yoga teachers often borrow it for the seer.

Either way the move is the same: the eating bird looks up. A feeling can be fully there, sweet or bitter, while something in you sees it. That's why many Hindu teachers describe meditation as learning to witness.

how: In classical yoga study, sutras 1.3 and 1.4 are read with the Samkhya distinction between purusha, the seer, and prakriti, the seen, and meditation is described as learning to witness the mind rather than be swept along by it.

o: the one who sees, behind the thoughts
a teacher who has seen the truth
a vision that comes in meditation

games.q: the two birds and the seer — tap the pairs.
p: happy or miserable with every bite
makes the clear crystal look red

s: for Patanjali, your thoughts are the seer
thoughts belong to what is seen. the seer is the awareness that sees them.
in the Upanishad, the eating bird's sorrow falls away when it looks up at the other
and many teachers read the watcher as the Lord, or the highest self.
Patanjali invented the seer-and-seen idea from nothing
he leans on Samkhya, a related Hindu school of purusha and prakriti.

games.q: a wave of anger arrives. according to thread four, what usually happens?
o: the seer takes the shape of the anger.
the anger disappears on its own.
games.why: otherwise, the seer takes the form of the turnings: it looks exactly like its thoughts.

practice: Let a thought come, any thought, and instead of following it, notice it the way the quiet bird watches the other one eat.
Each time, step back half a step: there's the thought, and here is the one seeing it; you don't have to name the seer, just notice that seeing is happening.
If you pray, you can rest in that quiet as a prayer, in the company of the Lord; if you don't, simply rest in the watching.

wordCard.voice: Drashta, the seer, the one who sees. When the turnings still, the seer rests in its own nature. Otherwise it takes the shape of its thoughts, like the bird lost in the fruit.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the seer, from drish, to see. Yoga Sutra 1.3 speaks of the seer resting in its own form.

carryVoice: Your line: you are the seer, not your weather. Two birds, one tree. Day two ninety-seven, done.

sources.ref: The crystal and the red flower (sphatika and japa flower), an image from the classical commentaries and Samkhya
Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1–3.1.2 (two birds on one tree; the eater grieves, and is freed from sorrow on seeing the other); the same two birds in Rig Veda 1.164.20 and Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.6–4.7
